newsitem.title: USA: Reebok awards spotlight human rights abuses.
newsitem.headline: Reebok awards spotlight human rights abuses.

text.p: Five young people from around the earth were honoured Wednesday for their work in protecting others at the ninth annual Reebok Human Rights Award ceremonies.

Julie Su was a winner. She is a 27-year-old Harvard educated lawyer who champions the causes of immigrant workers in southern California. She fought to free 72 Thai garment workers held in forced labour in a rat-infested El Monte, Calif. sweatshop.

"Manufacturers cannot take credit for the design, the quality the label and the product, and then not take responsibility for the conditions under which their products are made," she said after the ceremony.
Another winner, Jesus Tecu Osario, 25, exposed the rape, torture and massacre of 177 fellow villagers, including his three-year-old brother, in Rio Negro, Guatemala.

Speaking through a translator, Osario told the 1,000 member audience, "I call on you to pressure the U.S. government to declassify all information it has concerning massacres and other human rights violations in Guatemala."
Innocent Chukwuba, a 30-year-old Nigerian activist, won an award for publicising abuses by police despite being jailed twice by successive military regimes.

He dedicated his award, which comes with a $25,000 cash prize, to "the over 200 journalists, labour leaders, human rights and pro-democracy activists in Nigeria who are presently either in jail, driven underground or forced into involuntary exile abroad."

A Beijing Tiananmen Square democracy activist, Li Lu, a previous winner, presented a human rights award for Burmese activist Ma Thida, 29, a doctor and author who remains jailed by the State Law and Order Restoration Council.
To accept the award was a childhood friend, Myiang Myiang Nyunt who told the audience, "I want to thank you for thinking of her and I want to thank you for thinking of Burma."
Young activists honoured before have paid with their lives. Iqbal Masih, a 12-year-old Pakistani was murdered a few months after being named a 1994 Reebok Youth-in-Action Award winner.
Masih's death caused Craig Keilburger, 13, of Thornhill, Ontario in Canada, to travel to Sweden, Brazil, Haiti and southeast Asia to battle against child labour practices.
"The day that Iqbal died, a thousand new Iqbals were born. I stand here as just one of them," Keilburger said, adding that his being honoured showed children can have power.
